title: Antibody ID: Double Dose, and Kidd Comes Back
summary: See why some antibodies react more strongly with homozygous cells, why Kidd antibodies vanish and then cause delayed hemolytic reactions, and how rule-outs, the rule of three, enzymes and transfusion records catch them.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hit 3 (dosage; homozygous screening cells), Hit 5 (Kidd evanescence and delayed HTR), Hit 7 (enzyme effects) and Trap 1 (negative screen, later hemolysis). Checked against Manduzio 2024, Salarvand 2025 and Furqan 2026. Context added: Rh antibodies other than anti-D also show dosage; S/s react variably with enzymes (register flag rv-enzyme-ss). Pending: Kidd DHTR timing “5–10 days”.

objectives: Explain dosage and list antibody groups that show it.
Describe Kidd antibody evanescence and how it leads to delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.
Apply homozygous rule-outs, the rule of three, enzyme patterns and history checks in antibody identification.

scenes.title: A negative screen — then hemolysis a week later
scenes.altText: A patient with sickle cell disease, transfused at other hospitals before. Today’s two-cell antibody screen is negative and two units are given. Seven days later: dark urine, falling haemoglobin, positive DAT — anti-Jkᵃ is identified. How did the screen miss it?

cues.text: A patient with sickle cell disease, transfused elsewhere before, has a negative two-cell antibody screen today. Two units are given.
A week later: dark urine, falling haemoglobin and a positive direct antiglobulin test. Anti-Jk-a is identified.
How could a negative screen miss a dangerous antibody? Two Kidd tricks: dosage and disappearing.

props.label: How did the screen miss it?

scenes.title: Normal: double dose, stronger reaction
scenes.altText: Two schematic red cells. A homozygous Jk(a+b−) cell inherited Jkᵃ from both parents and carries a double dose (more Jkᵃ tokens); a heterozygous Jk(a+b+) cell carries a single dose. With a weak antibody, the homozygous cell agglutinates clearly and the heterozygous cell may react weakly or not at all. Antibodies that show dosage: Rh (except anti-D), Kidd, Duffy and MNS.

cues.text: Blood group genes come in pairs. A Jk-a-positive, Jk-b-negative cell got Jk-a from both parents — a double dose.
A Jk-a-positive, Jk-b-positive cell got one Jk-a gene — a single dose, with less Jk-a on its surface.
Some antibodies care about that difference. A weak antibody may clearly agglutinate the double-dose cell but barely react, or not react, with the single-dose cell. That is dosage.
Antibodies that show dosage include Rh antibodies other than anti-D, Kidd, Duffy and MNS.

props.title: Antibodies showing dosage
lines: Duffy (Fyᵃ, Fyᵇ) · MNS (M, N, S, s)

scenes.title: What changes: Kidd antibodies hide, then come back
scenes.altText: A graph of antibody level over time with a dashed “detection limit” line. After a first exposure, anti-Jkᵃ rises above the line, then falls below it within weeks to months (evanescence), so later screens are negative. On re-exposure to Jk(a+) cells, an anamnestic response drives it back up within days, and transfused cells are destroyed — intravascularly and extravascularly — a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction.

cues.text: After a first transfusion or pregnancy, anti-Jk-a appears. Kidd antibodies are often low-titre and weak to begin with.
Then they fade — often below the detection limit within weeks to months. Later screens come back negative, even though the immune memory remains.
Transfuse Jk-a-positive cells again, and memory cells respond fast. Within days the antibody surges.
The transfused cells are destroyed — both inside the blood vessels and in the spleen and liver. That is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction.

scenes.title: In the lab: rule out on homozygous cells, and use enzymes wisely
scenes.altText: Panel cards. Rule-outs for dosage antibodies use non-reactive cells with homozygous (double-dose) antigen expression — commonly at least two such cells (anti-K: one homozygous or two heterozygous). Rule of three: three antigen-positive cells reactive and three antigen-negative non-reactive to assign specificity. Enzyme (ficin) card: enhances Rh, Kidd, Lewis, P1, I; destroys M, N and Duffy; Kell unaffected; S/s variable. History card: previous transfusion records can reveal an antibody that is now undetectable.

cues.text: When ruling out a dosage antibody, use cells that are non-reactive and homozygous for the antigen — commonly at least two of them. A heterozygous non-reactive cell can hide a weak antibody.
To call a specificity, look for at least three antigen-positive cells that react and three antigen-negative cells that don’t — the rule of three.
Enzymes help too. Ficin enhances Rh, Kidd, Lewis, P1 and I antibodies, and destroys M, N and Duffy antigens. Kell is unaffected, and S and s vary.
And check the history. A previous record of anti-Jk-a means Jk-a-negative blood, even when today’s screen is negative.

props.label: Rule of three: 3 positive react · 3 negative don’t

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Anti-Jkᵃ ruled out on a non-reactive Jk(a+b+) cell” is crossed out → “Rule out dosage antibodies on homozygous cells.” Trap card: “Negative screen today = no clinically significant antibody” is crossed out → “Kidd antibodies evanesce — check history and records.” Trap card: “Antibody disappears with enzymes = anti-Jkᵃ” is crossed out → “Enzymes enhance Kidd; disappearance suggests Duffy, M or N.”

cues.text: Trap one: don’t rule out anti-Jk-a on a heterozygous cell. Dosage antibodies are ruled out on homozygous cells.
Trap two: a negative screen today doesn’t prove there’s no antibody. Kidd antibodies fade between exposures — check the history.
Trap three: if reactivity disappears with enzymes, think Duffy, M or N. Enzymes make Kidd antibodies stronger, not weaker.

scenes.title: Kidd hides and comes back
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Double dose, double reaction” and “Kidd hides, then comes back — the record remembers.” Plus “Enzymes eat Duffy, M and N; they feed Rh and Kidd.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: double dose, double reaction. Kidd hides, then comes back — so the record must remember. Enzymes eat Duffy, M and N, and feed Rh and Kidd.

Where it breaks: rule-out conventions differ between labs; anti-K can be excluded on heterozygous cells; S and s react variably with enzymes; and not every Kidd antibody evanesces, or causes a delayed reaction.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Dosage antibodies (Rh non-D, Kidd, Duffy, MNS): rule out on homozygous cells”, “Kidd evanesces → delayed HTR; enzymes enhance Kidd, destroy Fy/M/N; check records”.

cues.text: Rule out dosage antibodies on homozygous cells, remember that Kidd antibodies fade and then return to cause delayed hemolysis, and use enzymes and transfusion records to find them.

props.label: Dosage (Rh non-D, Kidd, Duffy, MNS) → rule out on homozygous cells
Kidd evanesces → delayed HTR · enzymes enhance Kidd · check records

explanation.what: Plain language: cells that inherited an antigen from both parents carry more of it, so weak antibodies react more strongly with them; Kidd antibodies can fade to undetectable levels and then return quickly. Scientific terms: dosage = stronger reactivity with homozygous (double-dose) than heterozygous cells, seen with Rh (non-D), Kidd, Duffy and MNS antibodies; Kidd antibodies are often low-titre, weakly avid and transient (evanescent), with anamnestic responses after re-exposure.
explanation.why: Antigen density determines whether a weak antibody produces visible agglutination. Evanescent antibodies drop below detection, so a later screen is negative, but memory B cells mount a rapid response when Jk-positive cells are transfused, causing intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.
explanation.measure: Rule out dosage antibodies on non-reactive cells with homozygous antigen expression (commonly ≥ 2; anti-K: one homozygous or two heterozygous). Rule of three: three antigen-positive reactive and three antigen-negative non-reactive cells. Ficin enhances Rh, P1, I, Kidd and Lewis; destroys M, N and Duffy; Kell unaffected; S/s variable. Review transfusion and antibody records; prior anti-Jkᵃ requires Jk(a−) blood.
explanation.differs: Homozygous vs heterozygous cells; enzyme-enhanced (Rh, Kidd, Lewis) vs enzyme-destroyed (Duffy, M, N) antigens; acute vs delayed (anamnestic) hemolytic reactions.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which antibodies show dosage, Kidd as the classic delayed HTR antibody, the 2-cell screen pitfall, enzyme patterns, and the rule of three.

left.label: Homozygous (e.g. Jk(a+b−))
points: Valid for ruling out dosage antibodies

mnemonic.explanation: Captures dosage, Kidd evanescence with anamnestic return, and enzyme patterns.
mnemonic.limitation: Rule-out conventions vary; anti-K can be excluded on heterozygous cells; S/s variable with enzymes; not every Kidd antibody evanesces or causes a delayed reaction.

questions.stem: A panel cell typed Jk(a+b+) is non-reactive. Can anti-Jkᵃ be ruled out on this cell?

options.text: No — Kidd antibodies show dosage; rule out on homozygous Jk(a+b−) cells
options.rationale: Correct. A weak anti-Jkᵃ may not react with a single-dose (heterozygous) cell.

options.text: Yes — any antigen-positive non-reactive cell rules it out
Yes, if the test used enzyme-treated cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Enzymes enhance Kidd but the heterozygous-cell limitation still applies.

options.text: No — anti-Jkᵃ can only be ruled out by DNA testing
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serologic rule-out on homozygous cells is standard.

questions.stem: Seven days after transfusion, a patient with a negative pretransfusion screen develops hemoglobinuria and a positive DAT. Which antibody is the classic cause?

options.rationale: Correct. Kidd antibodies are often undetectable before transfusion, then rise anamnestically, causing delayed hemolysis that can be intravascular.
Incorrect. Lewis antibodies are usually IgM and rarely cause hemolytic reactions.
Incorrect. Anti-P1 is usually a clinically insignificant cold antibody.
Incorrect. ABO incompatibility causes an acute reaction, not a delayed one after a negative screen.

questions.stem: An antibody reacts in the antiglobulin phase but stops reacting with ficin-treated panel cells. Which specificity is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Duffy antigens are destroyed by ficin, so the antibody no longer reacts.
Incorrect. Kidd reactivity is enhanced by enzymes.
Incorrect. Rh reactivity is enhanced by enzymes.
Incorrect. Kell antigens are unaffected by ficin.
